items.detail:
Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

The state’s Department of Education (FLDOE) said on Thursday it became aware of a data breach involving the Florida Student Financial Aid website on October 19.

Florida warned students that a recent data breach exposed sensitive information — including Social Security numbers and addresses — on nearly 5 million people who have applied for financial aid in the state.

The state’s Department of Education (FLDOE) said on Thursday it became aware of a data breach involving the Florida Student Financial Aid website on October 19. The information exposed includes names, addresses, phone numbers, genders, email addresses, Social Security numbers and dates of birth.

“An unauthorized party gained access to a system or database containing company or customer information,” the department said in a statement. “FLDOE is partnering with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement in its response to the event.”

FLDOE has taken the financial aid site down and warned that other department websites and services may experience temporary disruptions. Financial aid for students is not at risk and the breach will not delay aid disbursements or tuition payments. The incident will also not impact scholarships, grants or student loans.

The state urged those affected to monitor their credit reports and financial accounts for any irregular activity.

The department declined to comment about the nature of the incident or the attackers. The statement says the incident has been contained and was reported to the Office of the Attorney General.

This story is interesting: One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about. Among the pre-installed bloatware—­or spyware, if you’re being less charitable­—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go. It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.

The judge could block the sale of user data held by Character, which DOJ’s bankruptcy office notes has an “ambiguous” privacy policy suggesting it can sell at least some users’ chat histories.

Character is a “first-in-kind super intelligence entertainment platform that allows users to have immersive, multimodal experiences with fictional or imagined characters,” the office said in a Tuesday court filing .

The company currently has 12 million active monthly users worldwide and customers typically spend an average of two hours a day on the platform, according to the filing.

The Character chatbot tells users who ask if their conversations are private that they will not be shared, the filing said.

Signal de veille — The Record.

The company, billing itself as “the next-generation fashion retailer for Millennial and Generation Z consumers,” said a recent hack exposed customer payment card numbers.

Online fashion retailer Revolve warned investors that cybercriminals gained access to payment card numbers and expiration dates during a recent cyber incident.

The clothing giant filed an 8-K report on Thursday with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) saying hackers gained access to multiple company systems.

Revolve did not respond to questions about when the attack occurred but said in the report that an initial investigation found that the threat actors used “automated means” to obtain names, contact information, payment card numbers and payment card expiration dates from customers who saved payment information in their online shopping account on Revolve’s e-commerce platform.

Revolve said it has notified federal law enforcement agencies about the attack and has hired a cybersecurity firm to lead the recovery effort. There were no operational disruptions caused by the attack, and Revolve said it will not face material financial impacts as a result of the incident.

The company, which bills itself as “the next-generation fashion retailer for Millennial and Generation Z consumers,” did not say how many people were affected but told regulators in Texas on Friday that 127,200 people in the state had information stolen. Another 1,328 victims are in Vermont, and breach notifications were filed in Massachusetts .

items.body:
Signal de veille — The Register.

General Motors is taking what looks like a light slap on the wrist from a coalition of 35 states and the District of Columbia after agreeing to settle allegations that it collected drivers' data without proper consent and sold it to data brokers that supplied insurance companies.
items.detail:
Signal de veille — The Register.

General Motors is taking what looks like a light slap on the wrist from a coalition of 35 states and the District of Columbia after agreeing to settle allegations that it collected drivers' data without proper consent and sold it to data brokers that supplied insurance companies. The Washington state AG's office said on Thursday that GM had reached a $220 million settlement with 36 attorneys general over the automaker's collection and sharing of driving data, including precise location information, speed, seatbelt use, and other metrics. According to investigators, GM sold that data to brokers, which in turn supplied it to insurance companies that could use it to set customers' premiums, without drivers' informed consent. For reference, the $220 million settlement, which will be distributed among the participating jurisdictions, equates to less than 7 percent of GM's $3.3 billion in net income attributable to stockholders for its third quarter, which ended on September 30, 2026. Don't spend it all in one place, y'all. The settlement comes more than two years after a 2024 New York Times investigation found that GM had been selling the data collected from vehicle owners through its Smart Driver program. That program, part of GM subsidiary OnStar’s offering, collected the aforementioned data and handed it back to vehicle owners in reports designed to inform better driving habits.

Leading cryptocurrency analysts have attributed the cyber-attack to a North Korean elite hacking unit

According to a company statement on October 30, its investigation suggested that an attacker's entry point may have been a compromised Binance development and operations (DevOps) engineer's laptop.

This allegedly allowed the attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.

However, Binance has since revised that assessment and said its subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach.

"This was a complex attack," the company said, adding that it was working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other industry partners to establish the full circumstances as well as identify and recover affected assets.

Binance has not yet provided a definitive account of the attack, saying it is still gathering the facts and will publish a comprehensive technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete.

The company has said it has found no evidence that any wallet private keys were leaked.
